Subject: Throughput safety-net slate offer for OrionBio — options and asks

Hi Brian / Ops team —

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Attached is a short, decision-oriented packet with three distinct "slate" options that balance predictability and headroom for your peak inference patterns. High-level asks before we firm numbers into the term sheet:

- Can you confirm sustained steady-state tokens/sec for your main endpoint (estimate we discussed: ~180k tokens/min)?
- Which SLAs matter most: p95 latency under 250ms, or absolute tail (p99)?
- Are you planning to burst across regions (us-west + us-east) or stay single-region for launch?

Attached: 20260824-tsn-slate-offer.pdf (three slate constructs + warm-start/burst credit examples)

Quick summary of options in the doc:
- Guardrail Slate A: 24 min-active GPUs (baseline), 48 max with 2x burst credits. Fastest economics at steady-state; limited regional redundancy.
- Safety-net Slate B: 12 min-active / 36 burstable (recommended if you need cost/latency balance). Includes 20% warm-start headroom for KV-cache priming.
- Lightweight Slate C: 6 min-active, rely on regional geo-burst; good for pilot + short ramp.

Next steps we recommend: a 60-day pilot on Slate B with staged ramp windows (week 1: 25% baseline, week 3: 50%, week 6: full baseline). That gives ops time to tune batching and warm cache behavior.

If you prefer a single number for the term sheet, tell us which slate you favor and we will produce a priced term sheet + activation calendar.

Best,
Olga

Thanks for this. A couple of clarifying points before we pick a slate: 

1) For "min-active GPUs" do you mean permanently provisioned (billed) capacity, or can part of that be cold-stopped and billed as storage? We want to understand the monthly commitment profile.
2) On the Safety-net Slate B you listed 20% warm-start headroom. Is that an extra GPU pool or policy-driven cache pre-warm?
3) What does the burst credit burn look like if we have a large weekend job that spikes 4x for 2 hours?

Hi Brian — quick answers to your technical questions: 

On min-active GPUs: that is the minimum warmed allocation we keep ready (billed). We can offer a hybrid billing profile where a portion (up to 40%) is offered as "standby lanes" at a lower reservation price if you accept a slightly slower activation window (~10–15 minutes) — useful to reduce MRR during pilots.

Warm-start headroom: the 20% is policy + KV-cache pre-population. It is not a dedicated extra GPU pool, it is a mix of cache priming and prioritized placement that keeps slots ready for immediate continuation. That reduces cold-start token latency by ~30–50% in our internal measurements.

Burst credit model: burst credits are consumed from a capped pool (we model it as N GPU-hours per billing window). For example, Slate B with your projected profile: 36 burstable yields ~72 GPU-hours of burst credit per week. A 4x 2-hour weekend spike would use ~8–12 GPU-hours depending on model sharding; we can increase the credit pool for an additional one-time onboarding fee or convert to scheduled burst reservations.

Concrete recommendation for term sheet entries we can feed procurement: 
- Baseline billing: 12 min-active GPUs reserved (monthly commitment)
- Standby lanes: 6 GPUs at reduced reservation price (activates 10–15m)
- Burst pool: 72 GPU-hours / week included, extra hours billed at overage rate or via pre-purchased add-on blocks
- Ramp schedule: Week 1 (pilot): 3 reserved, Week 3: 6 reserved, Week 6: 12 reserved (move standby lanes into active as usage patterns stabilize)

I'll prepare a technical appendix with the warm-start expected gains and the example cost math for both monthly and annual commit. Olga / Marissa — can we get that priced for Orion's procurement cut on 8/27?

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Head of Capacity Planning | Redwood Inference
